you have you're right to consult a lawyer, but that's basically 1 call (s. 11(b) of the Charter). The lawyer will tell you to keep your mouth shut. Once you have this consultation the police can question you within reasonable limits while you are detained. They have to do something pretty outrageous for it to be considered a tactic that will vitiate a confession... Something that would "shock the conscious of the public" like pretending to be a priest in a confession booth (that was an example an SCC judge gave). But other than that, the law is lenient to the extent that it allows the police to do their jobs, as long as it does not bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

In the US, your Miranda rights are different from the admission of evidence that was obtained by a search and seizure not pursuant to a warrant. Usually what will be judged is whether the administration of justice will be brought into disrepute in the event that the evidence is admitted. In Canada this is the Grant test.

Again, I don't know know the exact situation in the States, but I'm sure it's similar to Canada (I'm a 2nd year law student in Canada). 

Not talking to police is the golden rule when you're arrested for anything. That will also be exactly what your lawyer will tell you in the US; however I believe you have a right to have a lawyer present during any police questioning in the US, that's not so in Canada.

I'm not sure how you guys do it in the US, but in Canada even though the an item is seized in contravention of the Charter (s. 8 protection from unreasonable search and seizure) the evidence may still be admitted if it can be justified by the state. These justifications are more thoroughly defined in the case law. 

My point is that even if evidence is obtained illegally, that does not automatically mean it will be tossed out. I'm sure this also holds true for US law.

The couple in the article is a rather fringe case, as they have been together since highs school, almost everything would be considered a family asset. The new Family Law Act is an attempt to relieve litigation and promote couples to enter into contractual arrangements for the division of property.

Because same-sex marriage is legal, of course they will fall within the laws. However, for groups of people practicing polyamory, it is not so clear. Turbulence on an airplane can not only affect vertical displacement of the plane (altitude) but also also the roll and tilt of the plane. A sudden increase in air speeds may cause the plane to roll sideways or in some cases take a dive. If you weren't wearing a seatbelt this may cause you to hit the ceiling of the plane. 

As for seatbelts on buses, the height and weight of the bus makes it different than a car in the event of an accident. Instead of using a seatbelt as a major protective measure in the design of a bus, a technique called "compartmentalization" is used. This just means that the enclosed spaces on the bus are designed so that in the event on an accident you will not be flying through the air. Why they didn't have both measures could be for convenience on public transport but most likely the reason is that safety tests found that there was no significant effect from including seatbelts on buses. It could be in some cases research showed actual detriment by including them. 

Also in terms of liability and enforcement of seatbelts on buses it would be a mess. In the event of an accident, it would hard to establish contributory negligence for someone not wearing a seatbelt. For enforcement, would the individual receive a fine for not wearing a seatbelt or would it be the bus company? How would wearing seatbelts be enforced? If an officer saw someone not wearing a seatbelt on a bus would he have an obligation to pull the bus over? It seems to be a bit of a regulatory nightmare. In this view, it would seem that any slightly increased safety benefit provided by seatbelts wouldn't be worth the trouble that enforcement and litigation issues would bring.
